subject: Economics
description: GST slabs, direct vs indirect tax, Finance Bill

questions.stem: GST (Goods and Services Tax) was rolled out in India on:

options.option_text: 1 April 2016
1 July 2017
1 January 2018
15 August 2017

questions.explanation: GST was launched at a midnight session of Parliament on 1 July 2017 — observed since as 'GST Day'. The 101st Constitutional Amendment Act (2016) enabled it. India has a dual GST structure: CGST (Union) + SGST (state) on intra-state supply; IGST on inter-state supply (collected by the Union, shared). Alcohol for human consumption and petroleum products are still outside GST.
questions.subject: Economics

questions.stem: Standard GST rates in India span four principal slabs. The highest GST slab (excluding cess) is:
questions.explanation: Principal GST slabs — 5 %, 12 %, 18 %, 28 %. A few items (luxury cars, tobacco, aerated drinks) carry an additional 'compensation cess' on top of 28 %, pushing the effective rate higher. Zero-rated — unprocessed food grains, milk, curd, educational services. The GST Council (chaired by the Union Finance Minister; state FMs are members) sets rates by consensus.
questions.subject: Economics

questions.stem: Which of the following is a DIRECT tax?

options.option_text: GST
Income tax
Customs duty
Excise duty

questions.explanation: Direct tax — borne by the person on whom it is levied; cannot be passed on. Income tax, corporation tax, capital gains tax, securities transaction tax are direct taxes. Indirect tax — ultimately paid by the consumer; collected by the seller / importer. GST, customs duty, excise duty (still on petroleum), state VAT on alcohol are indirect. Direct taxes are administered by the CBDT; indirect taxes by the CBIC.
questions.subject: Economics

questions.stem: In the Union Budget, the 'Finance Bill' primarily deals with:

options.option_text: Borrowing authority of the Union
Imposition, abolition or change in taxes
Allocation of funds to ministries
Appointment of financial officers

questions.explanation: The Finance Bill (Art 110 read with 117) gives effect to the Government's taxation proposals. It is introduced alongside the Budget; must be passed before the end of the relevant financial year. Allocation of funds happens through the Appropriation Bill (Art 114). The Finance Bill is a Money Bill (Art 110) — can be introduced only in the Lok Sabha; the Rajya Sabha has only a recommending role and must return it within 14 days.
questions.subject: Economics

questions.stem: The GST Council is established under which Article of the Constitution?

options.option_text: Article 256
Article 279A
Article 280
Article 110

questions.explanation: Article 279A — inserted by the 101st Constitutional Amendment (2016) — establishes the GST Council. Chair: Union Finance Minister; Vice-Chair: chosen from state FMs; Members: state FMs / ministers nominated by each state. Quorum: half the members. Decisions need a 3/4 majority (weighted: Centre 1/3, states 2/3 combined). Article 280 — Finance Commission. Article 110 — definition of Money Bill.
questions.subject: Economics

questions.stem: The Laffer curve illustrates the relationship between tax rate and:

options.option_text: Inflation rate
Tax revenue collected
Unemployment rate
Exchange rate

questions.explanation: Laffer curve (Arthur Laffer, 1970s) — an inverted-U showing that tax revenue first rises, then falls as the tax rate increases past an optimum. At 0 % and at 100 %, revenue is zero (no tax; no incentive to work). The curve is invoked to argue for tax cuts when rates are above the optimum. The actual 'optimum' point is disputed and varies by economy and period.
questions.subject: Economics

questions.stem: Under India's direct tax code, the slab rates for individual income tax have historically been set by the:

options.option_text: Reserve Bank of India
Finance Act passed each year by Parliament
Supreme Court
Central Board of Direct Taxes alone

questions.explanation: Income-tax slab rates are not in the Income Tax Act 1961 itself — they are fixed each year through the Finance Act (after Parliament passes the Finance Bill). This is why 'Budget Day' every February-March is when new slabs take effect from the coming April 1. CBDT administers the law (framing rules, procedure), but cannot set the slab rates on its own.
questions.subject: Economics

questions.stem: Which of the following commodities is kept OUTSIDE the ambit of GST in India and continues to be taxed by state governments independently?

options.option_text: Mobile handsets and accessories (attract 18% GST)
Alcoholic liquor for human consumption (state levy only)
Restaurant food and beverages (taxed at 5% under GST)
Cement and construction materials (attract 28% GST)

questions.explanation: Alcoholic liquor for human consumption is explicitly kept outside GST; states retain the exclusive right to levy excise duty and VAT on it. Petroleum products (petrol, diesel, ATF, natural gas, crude oil) are similarly excluded. Mobile handsets, restaurant food, and cement are all fully within the GST framework. A common error is confusing 'alcohol for industrial use' (which is under GST) with 'alcoholic liquor for human consumption' (which is not).

questions.stem: The GST Composition Scheme enables small taxpayers to pay a fixed percentage on turnover. Which of the following correctly states a CORE eligibility condition for opting into this scheme?

options.option_text: Annual aggregate turnover must not exceed ₹1.5 crore (₹75 lakh for special category states)
The business must be engaged exclusively in manufacturing of taxable goods
The taxpayer must file returns on a monthly basis without exception
The scheme is open to suppliers making inter-state outward supplies freely

questions.explanation: The turnover ceiling of ₹1.5 crore (₹75 lakh for special category states in the North-East and hilly regions) is the primary eligibility threshold. Composition dealers are expressly barred from making inter-state outward supplies (Option D is wrong). The scheme covers traders and manufacturers as well as restaurant services — it is not restricted to manufacturing alone (Option B wrong). Composition dealers file quarterly returns, not monthly (Option C wrong).

questions.stem: A registered dealer CANNOT avail Input Tax Credit (ITC) under GST for which of the following purchases, even if a valid tax invoice is held?

options.option_text: Raw materials used directly in the manufacture of taxable finished goods
Motor vehicles used for transportation of employees to the office
Capital goods used exclusively in the course of taxable production
Input services used for providing taxable output services to clients

questions.explanation: Section 17(5) of the CGST Act lists 'blocked credits' where ITC is specifically disallowed. Motor vehicles used for commuting employees fall under this blocked category (unless the business is in passenger transport, driving schools, or similar specific trades). Raw materials, capital goods for production, and input services for taxable output are all eligible for ITC. A common exam trap is assuming any business vehicle purchase gives ITC — it does not unless used for specified purposes.

questions.stem: Under GST law, a 'zero-rated supply' is treated differently from an 'exempt supply'. What is the CRITICAL distinction between the two?

options.option_text: Zero-rated supplies attract no GST and block the supplier's ITC claims entirely
Zero-rated supplies allow the supplier to claim a refund of ITC paid on inputs used
Exempt supplies cover only goods, whereas zero-rated supplies apply only to services
Zero-rated supplies are taxed at 0.1% under a special export notification order

questions.explanation: Zero-rated supplies (exports and supplies to SEZs under Section 16 of the IGST Act) are taxed at 0% but the supplier CAN claim a refund of ITC paid on inputs — unlike exempt supplies where ITC is blocked/reversed. This makes zero-rating commercially superior to exemption for exporters. Option A reverses the rule entirely. Option C is factually wrong — zero-rating covers both goods and services. Option D confuses the 0.1% rate for certain merchant exports with the zero-rated concept.

questions.stem: Under the Reverse Charge Mechanism (RCM) in GST, who is responsible for paying the applicable tax to the government?

options.option_text: The supplier deposits tax and later recovers it from the recipient via invoice
The recipient of the goods or services pays the GST liability directly to the government
The GST Network (GSTN) auto-deducts tax from the supplier's registered bank account
Both supplier and recipient share the GST liability in a 50:50 ratio under RCM

questions.explanation: Under RCM (Section 9(3) and 9(4) of CGST Act), the liability to pay GST is shifted from the supplier to the recipient. This applies in cases such as purchase from unregistered dealers (in notified categories), legal services from advocate to business, goods transport agency services, etc. The recipient pays the tax on a self-assessment basis and can subsequently claim ITC on it (if eligible). GSTN has no auto-deduction mechanism (Option C), and there is no 50:50 split under RCM (Option D).

questions.stem: The GST (Compensation to States) Act 2017 guaranteed states compensation for any revenue shortfall. Which year was designated as the BASE YEAR for computing the protected revenue at a 14% annual growth rate?

options.option_text: 2014-15 (the year the GST Constitutional Amendment Bill was first tabled)
2015-16 (the agreed benchmark year under the Compensation Act)
2016-17 (the year the CGST and IGST Acts were passed by Parliament)
2013-14 (four years before GST's July 2017 launch, as per Finance Commission norms)

questions.explanation: The GST (Compensation to States) Act 2017 explicitly designates 2015-16 as the base year. States' revenue from subsumed taxes in 2015-16 was multiplied by (1.14)^n each subsequent year to compute the 'protected revenue'. Compensation was to be paid for five years (up to June 2022). Option C (2016-17) is a common error since that is when the GST laws were passed, but the base year for revenue is 2015-16. Options A and D are incorrect and represent plausible-sounding but wrong milestones.

questions.stem: Section 15 of the CGST Act lays down the rules for determining the 'Value of Supply' on which GST is computed. What is the PRINCIPAL basis for this valuation?

options.option_text: Maximum Retail Price (MRP) printed mandatorily on the product packaging
Transaction value — the price actually paid or payable for the supply between unrelated parties
Wholesale price as declared in the manufacturer's annual price schedule filed with GSTN
Cost of production plus a statutory profit margin notified by the GST Council quarterly

questions.explanation: Section 15(1) of the CGST Act states that the value of a taxable supply shall be the 'transaction value' — the price actually paid or payable when the supplier and recipient are not related and price is the sole consideration. MRP-based valuation (Option A) applies only to a specific schedule of goods notified under the Legal Metrology Act, not as a general GST rule. Valuation rules under Rules 27–35 of CGST Rules apply only when transaction value cannot be determined (e.g., related-party transactions or non-monetary consideration). Options C and D have no basis in the CGST Act.
